system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2191-02-05 18:48:00 to 2191-02-07 16:25:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted for a right ureteral stone requiring surgical intervention. Given his mechanical aortic valve and chronic anticoagulation with Coumadin, he was admitted early for a heparin bridge. He underwent right ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy and stent placement on January 19 without complications. Postoperatively, he was transitioned back to Coumadin with overlapping heparin until his INR reached the therapeutic range of 2.5–3.5. His hospital course was uncomplicated, with stable management of comorbidities including diastolic heart failure, COPD, diabetes, and coronary artery disease. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up with his PCP for INR monitoring and urology for stent removal.
problems: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified
Heart valve replaced by other means

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Thompson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you came in because your INR was low. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my nurse from the anticoagulation clinic called my doctor and said my INR was 1.4. I think I missed a few doses of Coumadin—got my pills mixed up this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Since you have a mechanical aortic valve, it's very important your INR stays in the therapeutic range to prevent clots. That’s why you were brought in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I know. I didn’t realize how low it was until they called. I did take a few extra pills when I realized—before coming in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. It’s good you recognized it, but we prefer not to self-adjust. We’ve started you on a heparin drip to cover you while we safely bring your INR back up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. How long will I need the IV heparin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Typically two days. We’ll keep the heparin going while you take your regular Coumadin. Once your INR is stable and therapeutic for 24 hours, we can stop the drip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular dose is 8 mg most days, 6 mg on Tuesdays and Fridays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve restarted you on that schedule. Your morning labs showed your INR went up to 2.1, which is a good start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. I’ll be more careful with my pills going forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. We’ll keep monitoring your INR daily. Your other labs look stable—kidneys, blood count, and glucose are all okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My diabetes is under control with glyburide and metformin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood sugar was 145 when you arrived—within your usual range. We’re continuing your home meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my breathing? I’ve been using my inhalers at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lungs are clear. We’ll keep your albuterol and Combivent as needed. No signs of COPD flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My heart’s been okay too—no chest pain or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure and heart rate are stable. We’re continuing your Lasix, metoprolol, and ramipril. ECG shows no new changes—old inferior infarct, but nothing acute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that years ago. And the strokes—I haven’t had any new issues since the surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your neuro exam today is normal. No signs of new deficits. We’re keeping you on aspirin for stroke prevention as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. So I’ll be here two days, on heparin and Coumadin, until my INR is stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan. We’ll check your INR again tomorrow morning. If it’s still in range, we’ll continue on track for discharge the day after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. Your INR came back at 2.4 this morning—solidly in the therapeutic range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I can stop the heparin soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it for one more day as a precaution. We need 24 hours of therapeutic INR while on Coumadin before stopping the drip. You’re on track for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Any changes to my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes. Still on metformin, glyburide, Lasix, ramipril, metoprolol, Lipitor, and Zetia. All your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed a rash in my groin area lately—maybe fungal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I examined it this morning—it looks like a fungal infection. I’m prescribing clotrimazole cream, apply twice daily for 13 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, I’ll use that. And my Coumadin—will the dose stay the same after discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, back to your usual: 8 mg on most days, 6 mg on Tuesdays and Fridays. But we’ve adjusted the tablets for easier dosing—now using 2 mg tablets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So how many pills will I take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On 8 mg days, you’ll take four 2 mg tablets. On 6 mg days, three tablets. Much easier to manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And I need blood work the day after I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a coagulation panel—INR and PTT. Please call your PCP with the results. The anticoagulation clinic will follow up with dose adjustments if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any signs I should watch for—like bleeding or clots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Call your doctor or come back if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, vomiting blood, black stools, or any unusual bruising or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news, Mr. Thompson. Your INR is still 2.4, and you’ve had 24 hours in range. We’re discontinuing the heparin drip and preparing you for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. So I just go home and continue my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Resume all your home medications, including the new Coumadin tablets. Use the clotrimazole cream as directed. Get your blood work done tomorrow and call your doctor with the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me. I’ll be more careful with my pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay safe, and don’t hesitate to call if anything concerns you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave—any chest pain, dizziness, or bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel fine. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Discharge papers are ready. Nurse will review instructions and prescriptions with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Patel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson. Stay consistent with your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you around. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted due to a subtherapeutic INR of 1.4 while on chronic warfarin therapy for a mechanical aortic valve. The cause was likely missed doses due to medication confusion. He was started on a heparin drip and resumed his home warfarin regimen. His INR rose to 2.1 within 24 hours and reached 2.4 by discharge, allowing safe discontinuation of heparin. His comorbidities, including diabetes, COPD, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and chronic diastolic heart failure, remained stable throughout the admission. A groin rash was diagnosed as fungal and treated with clotrimazole cream. He was discharged home with instructions to resume all medications, monitor INR the following day, and follow up with his PCP and anticoagulation clinic.
